newsitem.title: MEXICO: U.S. vows to prevent Latin American arms race.
newsitem.headline: U.S. vows to prevent Latin American arms race.

text.p: American U.N. envoy Bill Richardson promised on Wednesday the U.S. would carefully avoid an arms race in Latin America now that a ban on the sale of high-tech weapons to the region has been lifted.
President Bill Clinton on Friday ended a 20-year ban on the sale of some warplanes and advanced weapons systems to Latin America, saying the region today is far more democratic.
Former President Jimmy Carter cut off such arms sales when military dictators dominated the region.

"We don't want there to be an arms race," Richardson told reporters in Latin America. "The United States will take (potential arms sales) case by case; it's not a policy where we're going to sell to any country at any time."
From New York, Richardson spoke to reporters linked by satellite from U.S. embassies in Mexico, Brazil and Chile.

Richardson, a former congressman from New Mexico and the son of a Mexican mother, became U.S. ambassador to the United Nations in Feburary after former ambassador Madeleine Albright became Secretary of State. He grew up in Mexico City.
"We'll determine the geopolitical and regional factors and the bilateral relations we have with democratic countries before taking any steps," Richardson said.

When the policy was announced on Friday, one senior U.S. official said the United States will "clearly not" offer advanced weapons to Peru and Ecuador, which went to war in 1995 over a long-standing border dispute.
Richardson also ruled out any arms sales to Cuba, which U.S. leaders continually identify as the only non-democratic nation in the hemisphere.
"We want to push for a dialogue among Latin American countries so that they talk in a mature way about what they want to do with future military purchases," Richardson said.
